narrative:
The model predicted a 63.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeded the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by their influence. Your family income bracket had the strongest impact, followed by your first-year law school grades, and then your LSAT score. 

Your middle family income pushed the prediction toward failure. While many accepted students also come from middle-income backgrounds, this category was less favorable compared to the upper-middle and high-income brackets that dominate among those who were admitted. Your first-year grades, which placed you in the 5th decile, also worked against you; accepted students averaged a stronger 6th-decile performance in their first year. Surprisingly, your LSAT score of 39 was actually better than the average of 37.2 among accepted students and pulled the prediction slightly toward passing. Your solid undergraduate GPA of 3.6, well above the accepted average of 3.23, and your plan to attend full-time likewise offered some positive influence, but they were not enough to overcome the top factors.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record in the coming year, particularly aiming for top-decile performance, and consider retaking the LSAT if you can raise it further. These steps would directly address the areas that most affected your current prediction. (248 words)
